name: Sakewa at Mankhim
when: Apr–May, from the Baisakh full moon (Ubhauli); a second gathering in late autumn (Udhauli)
summary: Sakewa is the great earth-worship festival of the Kirat Khambu Rai. On Mankhim hill above Aritar, the Rai community gathers at its Mangkhim temple, priests recite the oral Mundhum, and circles of dancers perform the Sili steps that copy birds, animals and the work of the fields.
body: Sakewa (also written Sakela or Sakenwa) is the main festival of the Khambu Rai, one of the Kirati peoples of eastern Nepal, Sikkim, Darjeeling and Kalimpong. The year in the Kirat tradition has two halves: Ubhauli, the going up, when birds and herders move uphill at the start of summer, and Udhauli, the coming down, before winter. Sakewa marks both. In Sikkim the spring festival begins on the Baisakh full moon and is a nine-day bhumi puja, a worship of the earth for good harvests and protection from storms and drought.

The Mangkhim at Aritar is a temple of the Kirat Rai: in the Rai language mang means deity and khim means house. Wikipedia's article on Mankhim notes that the community assembles here twice a year for Sakewa. A ritual leader, the nakchhong, recites the Mundhum, the oral scripture that tells how the ancestors came into the world, while dancers move in a wide circle to drums and brass cymbals. Many of the Sili movements copy animals, birds and the stages of rice farming, from sowing to harvest.

Sakewa has grown from a family and clan observance into a public festival in Sikkim, and the state now marks it with a holiday. Celebrations take place at Mangkhim temples across Sikkim, and the one on Mankhim hill is the best placed for travellers on the Silk Route. Exact dates follow the lunar calendar, so ask us in advance, and check current status before you travel.
tips: Dress modestly and ask before photographing dancers or priests; this is worship, not a show.
Join the outer circle only if you are invited in; many visitors are, and it is a warm moment.
Book Aritar or Mankhim homestays early for the festival days, as Rai families from across the region come home.

faqs.q: When is Sakewa celebrated in Sikkim?
faqs.a: The main Sakewa begins on the full moon of the Nepali month of Baisakh, which falls in April or May, and runs as a nine-day earth worship. A second observance, linked to Udhauli, comes in late autumn or early winter. Dates move with the lunar calendar each year, so ask us or the Mankhim temple committee for the exact days, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend Sakewa at Mankhim?
faqs.a: Yes, respectful visitors are usually welcome to watch the gathering and the Sili dances on Mankhim hill. Stay at the edge unless invited, keep voices low during prayers, do not walk through the dance circle, and ask before taking photographs, especially of priests and elders. Bring small cash if you wish to make an offering.

Sili is the circle dance performed during Sakewa. Dancers move together to drums and cymbals, and many of the steps imitate birds, animals and farm work such as sowing, weeding and harvesting rice. A leader sets the movement and the circle follows. It is a ritual act tied to the Mundhum, the Kirat oral scripture, not a stage performance.

faqs.q: How do we reach Mankhim for Sakewa?
faqs.a: Mankhim is above Aritar in Pakyong district, about 70 km and 3 hours by car from Gangtok via Rangpo and Rhenock. From Aritar it is a 15–20 minute drive up a steep road. No special permit is needed, so foreign travellers with a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit can attend. Stay a night in Aritar or on Mankhim hill to catch the morning rituals.

name: Losar at Aritar Gumpa
when: Feb–Mar, first days of the first Tibetan lunar month
community: Bhutia, Sherpa, Tamang and other Buddhist families
summary: Losar is the Tibetan Buddhist new year. At Aritar Gumpa, a Kagyu monastery above Lampokhari lake, and at village gumpas up the Silk Route, it is a quiet community occasion of prayers, butter lamps, new prayer flags and family visits rather than a staged spectacle.
body: Losar, which simply means new year, falls on the first day of the first month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in February or early March. In Sikkim it is celebrated by Bhutia, Sherpa, Tamang and other Buddhist families, and it is a state holiday. The days before are for cleaning houses and settling debts; the days of Losar itself are for prayer, new clothes, food and visiting relatives.

Aritar Gumpa, a monastery of the Kagyu order on the hillside above Lampokhari lake, is the main Buddhist temple for the lower Silk Route villages. Around Losar, families come up to light butter lamps, make offerings and hang new prayer flags, and monks lead prayers. Higher up, the small Gadenchoeling gumpa at Gnathang serves the herding families of Nathang Valley.

We are honest about what you will see: village gumpas mark Losar with prayer and community, not with big public mask dances. If you want a cham dance, ask us about the monastery calendars at Rumtek or in Gangtok for the same season. What Aritar offers is the feeling of a hill village celebrating its new year, khapse biscuits on every table and greetings of Losar tashi delek on the road.
tips: Walk clockwise around the gumpa and its prayer wheels, and remove shoes where asked.
Do not photograph monks or worshippers at prayer without asking first.
Late February is also a good time to see Aritar clear and dry, before the spring haze.

faqs.a: Losar starts on the first day of the first Tibetan lunar month, usually in February and sometimes in early March. The exact date shifts each year with the lunar calendar. In Sikkim it is a public holiday and Buddhist families celebrate for several days. Check the year's date with us, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there mask dances at Aritar Gumpa for Losar?
faqs.a: We do not promise any. At village gumpas such as Aritar, Losar is mostly prayers, butter lamps, offerings and family visits. The big masked cham dances in Sikkim are tied to specific monastery calendars, such as the Losoong and Guthor dances at larger monasteries. If a cham is important to you, ask us to match your dates to a monastery that holds one.

faqs.q: Can non-Buddhists visit the gumpa during Losar?
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors of any faith are generally welcome at Aritar Gumpa if they dress modestly, keep quiet during prayers, walk clockwise and ask before taking pictures. A small offering at the altar is welcome but not expected. If monks are busy with rituals, wait outside and enjoy the view over the lake.

faqs.q: Is February a good time to visit Aritar?
faqs.a: Yes. Aritar at about 1,450 m is cool but not freezing in February, with clear mornings and good views towards the high peaks. It is a quiet month with lower homestay rates. If you plan to continue to Zuluk and Nathang, keep spare days, as snow can close the upper Silk Route road. Check current status before you travel.

name: Maghe Sankranti on the Teesta
when: Mid-January, 1 Magh in the Nepali calendar (usually 14 or 15 January)
summary: Maghe Sankranti marks the first day of the Nepali month of Magh and the turn from the coldest weeks towards spring. Families bathe at river confluences, eat sweet til laddoos, yam and ghee, and visit elders. Rangpo, where the Rangpo river meets the Teesta, is the district's natural river town for it.
body: Maghe Sankranti falls on the first day of Magh in the Vikram Samvat calendar, usually 14 or 15 January, and is one of the main festivals of Sikkim's Nepali-speaking communities. It marks the end of the month of Poush and the start of longer days. The custom is to bathe in a river, ideally at a confluence, then share winter foods that warm the body: sesame and molasses sweets, boiled yam and sweet potato, ghee and chaku.

Rangpo sits where the Rangpo river joins the Teesta, at a spot called Rangpo Doban, and the town's riverbanks draw families on festival mornings. Upstream, Rorathang lies at the meeting of the Rangpo with the Reshi and Pachey streams. In Sikkim the best-known Maghe fair is the large mela at Jorethang in Namchi district; in Pakyong district the day is mostly about family, food and the river.

Mid-January is a fine time to travel in the low valleys: Rangpo at about 330 m is mild and dry while Zuluk and Nathang above may be under snow. Ask us if you would like to combine a festival morning at Rangpo with a trip up to Aritar. Local melas and their dates vary each year, so check current status before you travel.
tips: Try til laddoo, chaku and boiled tarul (yam) from home kitchens or small sweet shops.
Never swim at a confluence; the Teesta's currents are strong even in winter. Watch from the bank.
If you want a big fair, add a day for the Jorethang Maghe Mela in Namchi district.

faqs.a: Maghe Sankranti falls on the first day of the Nepali month of Magh, which is usually 14 or 15 January. It is a public holiday in Sikkim. Families celebrate on the day itself, and some river-bank fairs in the state run for several days around it. Check the exact date for the year, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is eaten at Maghe Sankranti?
faqs.a: Winter foods believed to warm the body: til laddoo made with sesame and molasses, chaku (hard molasses toffee), boiled yam and sweet potato, ghee and khichdi. Families share these with relatives and visit elders for blessings. Small shops in Rangpo and Rorathang stock til sweets in the days before the festival.

faqs.q: Is there a Maghe Mela at Rangpo?
faqs.a: Families gather by the Teesta at Rangpo and at river meeting points such as Rorathang, but the largest Maghe fair in Sikkim is the Jorethang Maghe Mela in Namchi district. Local fairs in Pakyong district vary from year to year, so we check before your trip. Ask us, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is January a good month to visit Pakyong district?
faqs.a: Yes, for the low and middle valleys: Rangpo, Rorathang, Pakyong, Rhenock and Aritar are dry and clear, with cool mornings. The upper Silk Route at Zuluk and Nathang may have snow and road closures, which is beautiful but unpredictable, so keep spare days. Check current status before you travel.
